newsitem.title: USA: Group faults pending U.S. campaign-finance plans.
newsitem.headline: Group faults pending U.S. campaign-finance plans.

text.p: A large public watchdog group contended Monday that all campaign finance plans pending in Congress fail to pass muster as real reform.

Tom Andrews, a former congressman and now an official of Citizen Action, told a news conference he expected a campaign funding plan to be introduced in Congress in the next few weeks that will be real reform based on public financing.

The Maine Democrat, whose group claims two million members, said the plan is based on an initiative approved by Maine voters last November for public financing of state elections starting in 2000. Maine would be the only state providing for full taxpayer-financed state elections.
He said he wanted a similar system approved for federal elections so candidates would not have to chase after money and more people would have a chance to get into politics.

Discussion of campaign financing picked up momentum this year after widespread reports of alleged improper contributions, many from foreigners to Democrats, now being investigated by Congress and the Justice Department.
Under the new Maine law, candidates would have to refuse all special interest and other large contributions and abide by other restrictions, but they would get public financing.

Andrews said all the pending congressional proposals, including a widely publicised one by Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain and Wisconsin Democratic Sen. Russell Feingold, do not get special interest funding out of politics nor encourage average people to run for office.
If a Maine-type plan were used nationally, "campaigns are going to be less expensive and not as long and they are going to be completely free of special interests," he said.

If any of the pending proposals in Congres pass, he said, "Everything continues that people hate -- the millions of dollars that candidates have to raise, the fundraisers going on every night Congress is in session, hours and hours that you have to spend on the phone, thousands and thousands of dollars you have to raise every week -- all of those features continue with any of the options that are being discussed."

Andrews, who lost a race for the Senate in 1994, estimated that public financing -- a highly controversial proposal when offered unsuccessfully in the past -- would cost some $1 billion for House and Senate elections.
